page: Amazon Web Services x8i.xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. The instance is built on the x86_64 architecture using an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor clocked at 3.9 GHz, providing 4 dedicated vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. Cache configuration includes 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and an extensive 480 MB L3 cache. It incorporates advanced vector instructions such as AVX-512, Intel AMX tile and int8 matrix acceleration, and hardware cryptography extensions. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of DDR5 system memory operating at 7 GHz, delivering an expansive ratio of 16.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. No local storage is bundled with the instance, and it includes no hardware GPU accelerators. Network connectivity provides a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps without complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Performance benchmarks reflect strong single-core execution alongside typical throughput limitations associated with a 4-vCPU footprint. In single-threaded assessments, the instance achieves high results, including a Geekbench single-core score of 2159.0, single-threaded gzip compression at 34.54 GB/sec, and bzip3 decompression at 14.38 GB/sec. Conversely, multi-threaded CPU results place in lower comparative percentiles, such as a multi-core stress-ng score of 4321.66 and Geekbench multi-core mark of 4963.0. Memory bandwidth benchmarks yield 38.67 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 29.22 GB/sec for writes. Database execution profiles register 2795.77 on PassMark database operations, while in-memory throughput achieves 7.67 million Redis SET operations per second.

From an infrastructure efficiency standpoint, the x8i.xlarge provides cost-effective access to large DDR5 memory capacities without paying for excessive CPU cores that an application may not utilize. Tradeoffs include modest network throughput at a 2 Gbps baseline and reliance on remote block storage due to the lack of local disks. The instance profile is designed for in-memory key-value databases such as Redis, caching layers, small to medium relational database instances, and enterprise application servers that require high memory allocations alongside moderate multi-threaded compute demands.
